title: AWS Lambda Now Runs GPU Inference with 48 Concurrent Invocations Sharing One Model per GPU
summary:
AWS Lambda now runs Event Functions on EC2 G-series GPU instances through Lambda Managed Instances, with up to 48 concurrent invocations sharing one model per GPU, vLLM and SGLang base images that need no handler code, and 90-minute asynchronous timeouts. Billing is the instance price plus a 9.75 percent fee; first hands-on tests report an eight-minute publish and no response streaming.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers

title: How Much Should an Agent Remember? Deployment Lessons from Self-Distilled Memory for LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents on long-horizon tasks fail in recurring, procedural ways. They mis-paginate an API, resolve the wrong entity, or answer when no answer was asked. We built a pipeline that lets an agent learn from its own history. It first mines short \emph{lessons} from the agent's own trajectories, one to three per episode. It then consolidates those lessons into a smaller set of \emph{guidelines}, where each guideline records how many lessons it merged. At inference the agent receives either all guidelines or a selected subset. The pipeline ships in the open-source altk-evolve library and is deployed in IBM's CUGA agent and watsonx Orchestrate platform. We report what we learned building, measuring, and productizing it. Our primary instrument is the AppWorld benchmark, across models spanning 40--92\% baseline task completion. The central finding is that the right amount of memory is a property of the model, not the memory. A strong model keeps improving as guidelines are added. DeepSeek-V3.2 gains +9.5 points of task completion and +16.1 points of scenario completion with its full 191-guideline set. A weak model gains less from the same full set than from a small selected subset. gpt-oss-120b starts at 39.9\% task completion. It reaches 51.2\% with all 199 of its guidelines but 55.4\% (mean of two runs) with a selected subset of about 29. Around that result we report what went wrong: a high-support guideline that backfired, provenance silently dropped during consolidation, a swallowed API error that failed every task while producing a plausible log, and a baseline confound that nearly produced a misleading comparison with a prior method. We distill these into recommendations for teams deploying agent memory.

title: ClosureBench: A Benchmark for Reasoning under Closure Assumptions
summary: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) often answer questions from incomplete records. Missing information might be interpreted as unknown or false, depending on the completeness of the source. Current evaluations fail to distinguish these two aspects, as they are usually interwoven with other reasoning demands. We present ClosureBench, a benchmark that tests whether LLMs follow the stated rules for dealing with missing information. Every base scenario is tested under OWA, CWA, and LCWA, and only the treatment of missing information changes between variants. ClosureBench provides a verified base benchmark as well as agent extensions for action choice, source scope, and updates. A model is considered correct on a base scenario only if it provides correct answers in all of its closure variants. Across 960 instances, overall accuracy can mask substantial closure mistakes. Models achieve overall accuracy from 71.18% to 99.86% across replicated runs, but their core switch accuracy, measured on the scenarios whose gold label actually changes with the contract, varies between 18.23% and 99.31%. Large discrepancies emerge under LCWA. For example, some agents choose unknown despite the prompt indicating that missing information should be treated as false. Our findings demonstrate that evaluations of AI agents should not only measure whether agents can reason over existing facts but also whether they use the appropriate assumption when information is absent.

title: VideoACE: Benchmarking Agentic Video Understanding through High-Frame-Rate Actions
summary: Agentic video understanding requires models to actively interact with video environments to gather evidence and form judgments. Evaluating this capability therefore requires assessing whether models can translate opportunities for interaction into better understanding. We introduce VideoACE, a benchmark for assessing video understanding under conditions that support sustained interaction. We focus on high-frame-rate action videos, where rapid, subtle changes make targeted observation especially valuable. The benchmark comprises 1,000 multiple-choice questions spanning six categories of fine-grained action understanding, accompanied by temporal evidence annotations and user hints screened for answer leakage. Its evaluation environment combines video inspection tools with a user simulator, allowing models to adjust temporal coverage, sampling density, and spatial detail, and to revisit evidence and revise their judgments under simulated user feedback. We evaluate single-pass observation, autonomous tool use, and tool use combined with user feedback to examine how effectively models exploit these opportunities. Evaluation of five models reveals distinct patterns in how they acquire evidence and respond to opportunities for further interaction. These findings establish VideoACE as a testbed for examining agentic video understanding beyond performance under a fixed observation setting.

title: Using a "chaos loop" to harden the Claude Docs launch: 60 server errors across billions of requests
summary: Claude Docs is a doc editor that you, your teammates, and Claude all work in together. We released Docs on September 16, 2026. This post is about the service that runs underneath it.
story_key: model:claude|title:using a chaos loop to harden the claude docs launch 60 server errors across bill
content_excerpt: Claude Docs is a doc editor that you, your teammates, and Claude all work in together. The interesting part is that a Claude session anywhere, from chat to Claude Code, can open the same doc and read, write, and comment in it live, right next to you. We released Docs on September 16, 2026. This post is about the service that runs underneath it. Three weeks before Claude Docs opened to the public, it was running as a proof of concept on a single node, used by a few thousand people inside Anthropic. We were racing toward an ambitious launch date, and our own estimate said we'd see millions of docs within the first few days. We launched on September 16. By September 22, people had created over 4.6 million docs. Across 2 billion requests we saw only 60 server errors, and we never had to roll back. The whole Docs service ran on about 50 memory-optimized pods. But honestly, this only worked because our frontier models have gotten much better recently (I used an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.2). In our experience, they can now stick with one goal through a run like this for weeks, which is what helped us hit launch scale in a tight timeline. A few thousand internal users on one machine told us nothing about whether the service would survive launch, and we obviously didn't have launch traffic to test with. We wanted real evidence to decide how fast we could roll out. So on September 4, about two weeks before launch, I had Claude drive a staging cluster that mirrored production at over a million synthetic docs a day and break core components on purpose. And then... I just left it running (I've included the full cost at the end of this article). My setup was pretty simple. The loop was a session in Claude Code that I left running: pick a scenario, run the harness, read the telemetry, propose a fix, ship it to staging, repeat. That session acted as a coordinator and handed most of the work to sub-agents. In the busiest week, that usually meant about 11 sub-agents running at a time, and 30 at the peak. The coordinator also talked to our internal variant of Claude Tag (beta) via the Slack MCP to learn from other infrastructure teams at Anthropic who had scaled similar services. Their agents checked our scaling approach for pitfalls they’d already hit. Each iteration looked the same. title: How Public Evals Work and Fail, and What Should Change
summary: How to read eval scores and what to question, from a teardown of 12 benchmarks.
story_key: story|title:how public evals work and fail and what should change
content_excerpt: As models ship faster, eval scores are often the first thing we learn about a new model. But how much weight should we put in them? In eight of twelve public evals studied, there’s evidence the grader failed work that should have passed. And even when the grader gets it right, many benchmarks measure what’s easy rather than what matters, and should instead focus on reliability, work velocity, multi-turn collaboration, etc. Here, we’ll cover the common patterns and principles, the errors models make, and where current benchmarks fall short. I’ll also share what we’re getting wrong and what should change, including why average pass rate isn’t enough and why dollars are the wrong measure of cost. Finally, we’ll walk through twelve evals: four on coding and science, six on knowledge work, and two on browsing and computer use. By the end, you’ll know what to trust in a benchmark and what to question. In addition, eval benchmarks are increasingly maintained like software. They ship versioned releases and accept fixes through issues and pull requests. Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 retired 30 tasks and revised 57 others, and Harvey LAB’s public set has grown from about 1,250 tasks to 2,010 since launching in May 2026. Like software, these releases can also introduce breaking changes—Terminal Bench can drop saturated tasks with each version, making scores hard to compare across releases. Deterministic checks over LLM judges. Code-based checks are reproducible and won’t shift rankings when a judge model is updated. DeepSWE and AutomationBench avoid LLM judges altogether, and Agents’ Last Exam goes to great lengths to minimize them. When an eval does need a judge—for a legal memo or clinical response—it narrows the judge’s job to binary yes/no rubric items rather than a holistic score. Graders check the outcome, not the steps. The intent is to allow any approach that produces the right result to pass. For example, Terminal Bench inspects the final state of the container and ignores the agent’s intermediate commands or console output. AutomationBench, OSWorld 2.0, and DeepSWE work the same way. All-pass scoring is common because partial work often isn’t usable. Under all-pass scoring, a task passes only if every test or criterion passes. DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, Terminal Bench Science, AutomationBench, and Harvey LAB score this way. As Harvey puts it, “there is no partial credit for catching most of the issues”—a report that flags eight of ten risks is incomplete, not 80% us

title: Inkling 2 Mini on vLLM: Day-0 Support for a Looped Model
summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini from day 0: a looped MoE that runs its middle layers three times, with per-pass KV caches, gated messages between passes, fused kernels and DSpark speculative decoding.
story_key: model:vllm|variant:mini|title:inkling 2 mini on vllm day 0 support for a looped model
content_excerpt: Thinking Machines announced Inkling 2 Mini today. vLLM supports it and its variable-loop research checkpoint, TML-d24-varloop-research , on day 0 on NVIDIA Blackwell, Hopper and DGX Spark. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped model: its middle 12 layers run three times per token with shared weights, each pass with its own KV cache and gated messages from the pass before. It is a multimodal MoE with 26B total and 3.5B active parameters, up to 1M tokens of context and a native DSpark speculator. We provide a Docker image with Inkling 2 Mini support, vllm/vllm-openai:inkling-2-mini . You can serve the model with: And the variable-loop research checkpoint, here with 2 passes and one KV cache shared across passes: Figure 1. The prelude and coda run once; the loop core runs three passes, each reading messages from the one before. Prelude, core, coda. The 24 layers split into a prelude (layers 0–5), a loop core (layers 6–17) and a coda (layers 18–23). The prelude and coda run once each; the core runs three passes with shared weights, and the coda continues from the last pass. Each group of six layers is one block of the block attention residuals used in Inkling 2 Small, so one pass of the core produces exactly two blocks. Every pass starts from the prelude's output. A plain looped model feeds pass p's output into pass p + 1. Here, all three passes start from that same output, and pass p + 1 sees pass p only through messages. Messages are read at every sublayer. From the second pass on, each core sublayer input (the attention's query, key and value inputs and the MLP input) gets its own message, read from the previous pass's two blocks by an attention-residual read with a learned query per layer and input type. A rank-64 controller then merges the message into the input, per channel: With 12 core layers and 4 inputs each, every later pass reads 48 messages per token. Because the query, key and value inputs get different messages, the sliding-window layers, which project all three from one input in the first pass, take three separate inputs in later passes. Each pass keeps its own memory. Every core layer has a KV cache and a conv-state cache per pass, so pass p attends to the keys and values that pass p computed for earlier tokens. The model has 24 layers but 48 KV caches and 48 conv-state caches. DSpark draft from inside the loop. The 3-layer DSpark draft reads the target's hidden states at four layer visits: one in the prelude, one each in the second and third passes, and

title: Genie 4 is now available
content_excerpt: Explore a new Project Genie experience for Google AI Ultra subscribers, featuring Genie 4, the Project Genie agent, and a community gallery. We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, offering more responsive, social, and interactive world generation. You can now use natural language to edit environments in real time, add native audio, and share your creations in our new community gallery. Visit the Project Genie website to start building your own worlds or join the waitlist if you are a Google AI Pro member. Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie , an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them. So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds. Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser. With Genie 4 , our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. Today’s Genie 3 updates include: Genie 3 uses real-time promptable events to connect different worlds into one continuous flight across forests, underwater ruins, and icy seas. See how 360-degree panorama grounding in Genie 3 keeps Petra’s canyon and facade consistent as you look around.   • Added sign-in to organizations managed in Anthropic's Enterprise Admin Console: after claude auth login, Claude Code applies the organization's settings and uses its cloud provider or gateway
  • Added easel, a built-in mod that draws charts when asked and under MCP metrics results, on Pro, Max and, where available, Team and Enterprise on macOS and Linux; turn automatic charts off in /config
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_FULL_SIGN_IN_LINK=1 to print the full sign-in link, if the short one shows an error or a script reads values from it
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --start-dir / SELF_HOSTED_RUNNER_START_DIR to have Claude start its work in a folder of a repository, while settings and hooks load as without it
  • Added a notice in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions when a plugin marketplace can't be fetched because its repository isn't one of the session's
  • Self-hosted runner: Added a notice when Anthropic-managed git refuses a plugin's own repository, naming the plugin and what to do

  • Fixed /install-github-app and /design-login showing a generic failure for an account on hold instead of the on-hold notice and appeal link
  • Fixed a running MCP task being reported as stopped when you move a session to the background; the background session can now follow the task, but not if its server uses stdio or sets headers
  • Fixed self-hosted runners ignoring a session until they exited, after its failure report was lost or the session was given back to the same runner
  • Fixed self-hosted sessions losing the prompt cache and earlier thinking when the list of repositories a restart couldn't prepare changed
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed tool calls behind a permission prompt vanishing with no result when a new runner took over the prompt, in sessions with telemetry off
  • Fixed resumed self-hosted runner sessions starting without their pushed work in large repositories when --push-outcome-on-release is set
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions being shown as working when Claude Code hangs at every start and --startup-timeout-min is from 2 to about 6
  • Fixed pkill -f in self-hosted runner sessions on Linux ending its own shell with exit code 144, or the runner (needs a pkill with --ignore-ancestors)
  • Fixed scheduled tasks on self-hosted runners having no tool to notify their owner when telemetry is off or a third-party provider is used
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed one slow spawn-runner hook keeping the orchestrator from claiming sessions for its free slots; it now polls every 4 to 6 seconds while a slot is free
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a 403, such as an IP allowlist's, logged as a bad secret or token: most such lines now lead with the server's reason, so update log alerts that match the old words
  • Fixed self-hosted runners' warn mode for repository settings stopping at the first finding of most kinds: it now goes on, up to 50 for a session, and says if it stops early
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed runners that start on a full disk taking sessions and failing them; they now wait for room and exit 1 after a minute with no session, unless started from a work order
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a failed start suggesting a retry when the runner's machine had no git credentials; the error now says whom to ask and what to do if the repository is wrong
  • Fixed the self-hosted runner's last_poll_age_seconds reading 0 while the runner had never polled successfully
  • Fixed the notice about a skipped scheduled task that names no organization: it now says to start Claude Code with --resume, because /resume inside a running session doesn't run the task
  • Fixed claude plugin validate wrongly warning that a mod's AbovePrompt or AbovePromptList hook never runs in VS Code
  • Fixed /design-sync deleting a file it had just uploaded when Claude Design stored that file under a changed name
  • Reverted 2.1.329's removal of the automatic retry when max_tokens exceeds a model's or gateway's limit
  • Improved the claude.ai sign-in link shown by /login, claude auth login and claude setup-token: it is now much shorter
  • Windows: Improved Grep and Glob speed by no longer starting a console host for each built-in ripgrep search on a local path
  • Improved the speed of file diffs
  • Improved /config search: most settings whose name starts with what you type come first, "effort" finds Model, and "dark" or "light" finds Theme
  • Improved /resume: sessions where you only opened a screen such as /model and left are no longer listed
  • Improved Reconnect in /mcp and /plugin: a server's page now stays open, with the cause in view, when the server still fails or needs sign-in
  • Improved the error on macOS when sandbox deny lists are too long: it now names the long lists and how to shorten them
  • Improved /plugin in fullscreen mode: the page of a plugin with errors now starts with those errors
  • Improved /ultrareview's cost confirmation on Team and Enterprise plans: it now says how much of your monthly spend limit is left when that is less than a review usually costs
  • Improved self-hosted runner sessions on Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud's Agent Platform to say so when they start on another default model because your account refused the first
  • Windows: Improved the error when a session's folder is on a drive Claude Code can't verify: it says why, and whether retrying can help
  • Improved Code Mode: Claude is now told how to look at images and PDFs
  • Improved Code Mode: after Esc, "Interrupted" now shows under the stopped command in place of a red error
  • Improved Code Mode: the terminal freezes for far less time after a subagent's script makes thousands of tool calls
  • Changed recurring scheduled tasks and /loop to run up to 30 days instead of 7 while their session keeps running, and say when they end; tasks made before this release still end at 7 days
  • Changed more rm commands aimed at the root, home, a top-level folder or the working folder to ask for approval; where nobody can answer, they're refused
  • Changed deniedMcpServers name entries to hide only the named claude.ai connector, not others at its URL; to block them all, deny its exact URL
  • Changed claude --teleport in some setups to print the git commands for switching branch instead of running them; with -p it exits 1 until you switch
  • Changed unrecognized model names containing "sonnet" or "haiku" to use the shorter system prompt, like other unrecognized names; CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0 gives every model the full one
  • Changed skills that Claude runs with a model setting, other than context: fork skills, to leave subagents, forks, compaction and /recap on the session's model
  • Changed a subagent's model fallback to carry over: agents with no model and forks it then starts run on the fallback, and the agents they start use its Bedrock region
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed spawn-runner hooks to start while earlier ones still run, up to --hook-concurrency per orchestrator (4 by default); set it to 1 if yours can't run beside another
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed Bash commands to skip the file diff when nothing needs it, so transcripts can lack it; set bashEditDiffEnabled to true in managed settings to get every diff
  • Changed self-hosted runners to stop a session's start at once, without trying other runners, when a checkout hook exits with status 108
  • Changed prompt hooks to accept model aliases such as haiku or sonnet in their model field
  • Changed /design-sync's fallback build of the reference Storybook to use only a Storybook installed in the project
  • Changed subagent progress summaries in terminal sessions signed in to a Claude apps gateway to be written from short notes instead of the whole conversation, using far fewer tokens
  • [VSCode] Added /fork to fork a conversation after its last reply (#69272)
  • [VSCode] Added /workflows, which opens the agent map with running workflows
  • [VSCode] Added the claudeCode.escapeStopsClaude setting; turn it off so Escape does not stop Claude (#91536)
  • [VSCode] Added the claudeCode.pinPrompt setting to let your message scroll away instead of staying pinned
  • [VSCode] Added the claudeCode.contextUsageThreshold setting for when the context indicator shows (#93036)
  • [VSCode] Added a prompt argument to the "Open in Side Bar" command for keybindings and extensions
  • [VSCode] Added Move up and Move down to a session group's menu (#98654)
  • [VSCode] Fixed VS Code opening and focusing its terminal on every prompt of a connected terminal session
  • [VSCode] Fixed copying a code block adding a trailing newline that ran the command on paste (#96976)
  • [VSCode] Fixed holding Enter on /rewind restoring files, and a double click on Remove or Delete removing a memory, MCP server or plugin marketplace, without confirmation
  • [VSCode] Fixed Enter on a question card sending your earlier answer instead of picking the focused one, and arrow keys not working after an "Other" answer; answered questions reopen on your pick
  • [VSCode] Fixed a held-down Enter key sending a half-written message or running a typed slash command
  • [VSCode] Fixed Cmd+A, C, V, X and Z not working in the rename box and dialogs on macOS
  • [VSCode] Fixed Ctrl+F and Ctrl+P not moving the caret in the message box on macOS
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Accept and Reject buttons doing nothing on a proposed diff moved to a new window
  • [VSCode] Fixed Accept and Reject Proposed Changes showing over the chat, the terminal tab and other files; they now show only on the proposed diff
  • [VSCode] Fixed a slow-starting Claude tab taking the keyboard away from the file you had gone on typing in
  • [VSCode] Fixed unsaved changes and new problems being missed on macOS and Linux for files whose path contains #, ? or %20, such as a C# folder
  • [VSCode] Fixed whole-line selections counting one line too many in the selection chip, in @-mentions and in what Claude is told, and file links leaving out the last line of a range
  • [VSCode] Fixed a conversation forked in the panel re-running an old, unanswered prompt by itself after a window reload
  • [VSCode] Fixed a forked conversation running the original conversation's /loop schedules a second time
  • [VSCode] Fixed /clear giving no sign that the session still runs without a newly trusted folder's CLAUDE.md and settings
  • [VSCode] Fixed dialogs closing, and losing typed text, when a text selection was dragged past their edge
  • [VSCode] Fixed advisor calls showing as "Unsupported content type" (#73499, #64158, #90471, #73637)
  • [VSCode] Fixed the session list showing no status for the sidebar chat's session (#93898)
  • [VSCode] Fixed the plan preview's Add Comment button vanishing after a fast double click on a word
  • [VSCode] Fixed long lines cut off in the Edit Notebook Cell row, permission rules squeezed in a narrow panel, hard-to-see question card marks, and menus moving the chat after a declined trust prompt
  • [VSCode] Fixed signing in to an account on hold showing a generic failure instead of the on-hold notice and appeal link

title: An updated Clairic and Clairic-flash are now open-weight, from the new Workers AI Superintelligence team
summary: Clairic graduates from preview, while Clairic-flash joins the repertoire on Workers AI. We’re doing an open-weight release for both extraction models.
story_key: story|variant:flash|title:an updated clairic and clairic flash are now open weight from the new workers ai
content_excerpt: Cloudflare has become a neolab. We’re building our own frontier AI models for our customers and the open-source community. Both extraction models are hosted on Workers AI and full open weights are available on Hugging Face . We’re also excited to re-introduce ourselves as the Workers AI superintelligence team, the frontier AI research team behind Clef , Clairic, and lots more in the works. This team is working quickly to push the AI frontier and build useful models for Cloudflare’s customers and the open source community. Since announcing Clairic in preview, we have received a ton of use cases and helpful feedback on how customers wanted to use an extraction model. We heard about use cases ranging from extracting data from images like receipts to reading values from support tickets. We knew that we wanted extraction to be the clear focus for the model, so it had to excel at reading from unstructured data. We decided to go back to the drawing board with Clairic and redesigned our architecture, differentiating this new version of Clairic from our preview release. For ordinary text and number extraction fields, we now use parallel slot autoregressive generation instead of a single forward pass. Each field uses the tokens it has already written to choose its next token, then stops at its own end marker. All the fields advance together in the serving batch, still giving lightning-fast latency per request. This boosted our accuracy in extraction for both text and images, and the trade-off in accuracy offsets the small latency cost. For computation, estimation, and extraction use cases, we trained special heads that can handle estimates, forecasts, durations, calculated dates, and explicit arithmetic. Although the model architecture evolved, we kept the parts of the typed API interface that make the answers useful: confidence scores, character spans, and probabilities are still intact with every request. The model is still incredibly fast and cheap. From the evals below, you can see how our newer versions of Clairic have greatly improved on extraction across text, images, PDFs, and more. There are no public extraction benchmarks yet, but we ran our internal evals for other emerging extraction models on the market, such as Liquid AI’s D1.2 (pipelined with Apple Vision for optical character recognition) and Scaledown’s Extract . Our Clairic models excel across extraction use cases, but take these evals as directional guidance since they are self-reported. We wanted

title: Introducing managed cluster extensions for observability and user management in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm
summary: Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now offers managed cluster extensions for observability and user management, bringing declarative, API- and console-driven configuration to the software running on Slurm cluster nodes. This post explains how the extensions work and follows a platform team through a quarter of running a shared Slurm cluster with them.
